What I found especially interesting in this podcast was the argument that cyber threats will sustain demand for frontier models.

To defend against attacks that are one step below the frontier, you need a frontier model, which means investment in frontier models has to continue.

It is also interesting that corporate security officers are already worried that anyone can use a powerful open model to attack a company or hold it hostage.Jukan (@jukan05)I learned a lot from this podcast episode.

You should all watch it.

To share the insights I took away:

1. Even if you secure additional GPUs or memory, total system output cannot increase if other segments such as substrates, MLCCs, and wafer testing are in short supply. In other words, in the semiconductor industry, total shipments are determined by the single most constrained component or process.

2. Substrate, power and analog semiconductor, foundry, and memory suppliers have historically been conservative and have not made new greenfield investments until they were confident in long term customer demand. In response, Broadcom, Nvidia, and others signed sufficiently long LTAs with their supply chains and gave them visibility, and that point in time was precisely late 2025 to early 2026. Working backward from there to when a new production fab comes online, meaningful new capacity ramp and production will begin in 2028, not 2027. That means next year, 2027, could be the most supply constrained year in history.

3. In 2028, supply will still be short and the shortage will not be fully resolved, but it will be the year when the largest amount of new production capacity in the history of the semiconductor industry comes online at once. This is an opportunity for additional revenue.

4. The current supply constraint is a safety net that delays overinvestment. In past capital intensive infrastructure booms such as railroads, canals, 3G, and mobile phones, people always overbuilt. But the difference between past cycles and this AI infrastructure cycle is that even with demand in place, production facilities and data centers cannot be built as quickly as desired. So the current supply constraint can paradoxically be seen as playing a positive role in the sense that it limits excessive investment. The explanation is that by the time the supply chain catches up (2028), demand and industry conditions may have normalized to some degree as well. In enterprise AI too, high token costs and limited access to compute are slowing the pace of deployment, and if costs were much lower, companies would have moved more experiments into production environments faster.—  https://x.com/jukan05/status/2097618417067205107

items.content:
Samsung Electro-Mechanics and LG Innotek push to commercialize substrates for Intel's 'EMIB-T', challenging Japan's Ibiden

Samsung Electro-Mechanics and LG Innotek are pursuing the supply of high value added semiconductor substrates for Intel's Embedded Multi-die Interconnect Bridge (EMIB). EMIB is an advanced packaging technology whose demand has recently been growing in the high performance artificial intelligence (AI) semiconductor market. Japan's Ibiden is the leading company in this field.

According to industry sources on the 9th, Samsung Electro-Mechanics and LG Innotek are developing and testing products with the goal of entering the package substrate supply chain for Intel's EMIB-T.

Intel's EMIB-T gains traction in the AI chip market, drawing interest from Samsung Electro-Mechanics and LG Innotek

EMIB is an advanced packaging method that has recently been drawing attention in the AI semiconductor industry. Currently, the industry inserts a thin layer called a silicon interposer to connect high bandwidth memory (HBM) and system semiconductors into a single package. Using an interposer allows the circuits of each chip to be connected more densely. This is commonly referred to as '2.5D packaging'.

EMIB connects chips to one another using small silicon bridges instead of an interposer. It is a technology that places silicon bridges only where they are needed. It is more cost efficient than an interposer. Another advantage is that chips can be placed with more flexibility.

Because Intel had previously used EMIB only for manufacturing its own chips, market demand was limited. However, with Intel recently developing an improved version called 'EMIB-T', external sales are now expanding in earnest. Google will also apply EMIB-T for the first time in its next generation AI accelerator (TPU), scheduled for release in the second half of next year.

EMIB-T is a technology that inserts through-silicon vias (TSVs), which serve as power delivery pathways, into the silicon bridge. By shortening the power delivery path between the substrate and the chip through TSVs, it improves power efficiency and signal integrity.

Samsung Electro-Mechanics and LG Innotek have also taken note of the growth of EMIB-T and are attempting to enter the supply chain for its dedicated package substrates. The product embeds a silicon bridge into a flip chip ball grid array (FC-BGA), the existing package substrate for high performance semiconductors, making it technically demanding.

In the case of Samsung Electro-Mechanics, the company is developing the substrate under the concept of a 2.1D package substrate. A person familiar with the matter said, "Samsung Electro-Mechanics has been developing substrate samples for EMIB for several years, and following the recent trend toward EMIB-T commercialization, it is actively pushing to enter the supply chain."

LG Innotek recently sent package substrates for EMIB-T to SK hynix, which is conducting sample tests. LG Innotek and SK hynix are reportedly mounting HBM on the substrate and evaluating the product's characteristics.

Challenging FC-BGA leader Ibiden of Japan, but large scale investment is a burden

Entering the package substrate supply chain for Intel's EMIB-T is one of the key tasks for Samsung Electro-Mechanics and LG Innotek in expanding their high value added FC-BGA businesses, which is their goal.

Currently, package substrates for EMIB-T are supplied by four companies: Ibiden and Shinko Electric of Japan, Unimicron of Taiwan, and AT&S of Austria.

Ibiden is the number one company in the FC-BGA industry. It has built a solid cooperative relationship with Intel. In the first half of this year, it decided to begin construction of a mass production line dedicated to substrates for Intel's EMIB-T, utilizing an existing idle fab. The investment is approximately 2 trillion won. It is reported to have received advance payments from Big Tech companies including Google, Amazon, and Intel.

As latecomers to the relevant supply chain, Samsung Electro-Mechanics and LG Innotek are expected to have to overcome technological and market challenges in order to commercialize substrates for EMIB-T.

An industry official in the substrate sector explained, "Ibiden, Unimicron, and others have built stable technological capabilities and production capacity by mass producing substrates for Intel's EMIB for seven to eight years," adding, "It is true that business opportunities are expanding with EMIB-T, but domestic companies face the risk of having to make large scale investments first."

items.title: Now you see why SK hynix is looking to work with Intel, and why CXMT is hiring logic foundry engineers, right?
items.content:
Now you see why SK hynix is looking to work with Intel, and why CXMT is hiring logic foundry engineers, right?Jukan (@jukan05)SK hynix: "Foundry processes could be used for 3D DRAM"

SK hynix said on the 9th that it could use foundry processes in developing 3D DRAM, a next generation memory chip.

At the 2026 SK hynix Future Forum held the previous day at the SUPEX Center on the Icheon campus, SK hynix vice presidents Kim Kyunghoon and Son Hoyoung presented the use of logic foundry processes for DRAM peripheral circuits, maximizing data bus bandwidth, and ultra short distance transmission as the key technology directions for 3D DRAM.

3D DRAM is a next generation DRAM that increases density by stacking memory cells vertically instead of laying them out on a single plane (2D).

Kim and Son explained that realizing this technology requires solving not only design and heat issues but also packaging challenges such as fine interconnects, bonding, and process integration. They also expected that as the boundaries between front end and back end (packaging) processes, and between foundry and memory technologies, draw closer together, joint optimization that goes beyond existing domains will become important.

"3D technology is changing even the technical boundary between the fab and packaging," Son said. "Along with innovation in advanced packaging technology, it is important to build optimization that crosses existing domains and new systems of collaboration."

Shin Changhwan, a professor at Korea University who spoke on the same topic, said, "3D DRAM goes beyond simply stacking chips vertically. It is a technology that breaks down the boundary between memory and logic. With device scaling approaching its limits and the time and power consumed by moving data between the system and memory increasing, the shift to 3D technology is inevitable." He proposed a 3D integrated design framework that links four areas, materials, devices, packaging, and architecture, through artificial intelligence (AI).

In his opening remarks, SK hynix CEO Kwak Nohjung said, "If the memory market of the past was a straight road where the competition was about who could run faster, today it is like driving on a winding road that changes moment to moment. What matters is not only internal capability but also the speed at which we read the pace and direction of change in the external environment and adapt flexibly."—  https://x.com/jukan05/status/2097560788806640078 
— Jukan (@jukan05) Sep 9, 2026

Micron, Semiconductor Substrate Makers Show Interest in JDI's Mobara Plant Sale

Japanese display maker Japan Display Inc. (JDI) has drawn interest in the sale of its Mobara plant (fab), which halted operations this March, not only from Micron of the United States and several data center operators but also from a semiconductor substrate maker, according to sources on the 8th.

The JDI Mobara plant previously produced sixth generation liquid crystal displays (LCD) and organic light emitting diodes (OLED). It also mass produced OLED panels for the Apple Watch until the second half of 2025. As JDI had announced in the first quarter of 2025, it halted operations at Mobara in March 2026.

Industry source A said, "Micron and several data center operators have submitted letters of intent to JDI to acquire the Mobara plant." Another source B said, "Micron and a Korean semiconductor substrate maker, among others, are in talks with JDI over purchasing the Mobara plant." At its quarterly earnings announcement in early August, JDI stated that it was in discussions with multiple companies regarding the sale of the plant.

The reason Micron, data center operators, and semiconductor substrate makers are interested in the Mobara plant comes down to time. Building a new plant from scratch and securing government permits would take years before mass production could begin. Buying the Mobara plant shortens that timeline accordingly.

Because Mobara previously produced sixth generation LCD and OLED panels, its cleanroom cleanliness levels make it unsuitable for semiconductor front end processing, but the site can be used as a data center or as a back end packaging plant for products such as glass substrates. That is why Micron, data center operators, and substrate makers are interested. The sale price for the plant is currently reported to be under discussion at around KRW 500 billion, though the figure could change depending on circumstances.

OLEDWorks, a US OLED company working with JDI, is reported to be interested not in the Mobara plant but in the 4.5 generation Ishikawa plant. Ishikawa has a line capable of backplane (BP) processing. For OLEDWorks, securing a plant that can reliably handle BP processing going forward is a necessity.

JDI is currently considering selling its plants, including Mobara and Ishikawa, separately to different buyers. If each of these deals goes through, the ownership of JDI's plants would change hands individually.

JDI was formed in 2012 under the lead of the Japanese government (Innovation Network Corporation of Japan) by consolidating the LCD businesses of Sony, Toshiba, and Hitachi. It subsequently failed to respond to market shifts such as the growing adoption of OLED in smartphones and fell behind Korean and Chinese panel makers in competition. In November 2024, JDI unveiled a new catchphrase, "Beyond Display." Whereas the old JDI consisted solely of displays, the company said the new JDI would comprise displays, sensors, artificial intelligence (AI) data centers, and advanced semiconductor packaging.

Meanwhile, most of the equipment related to eLEAP, the technology JDI had developed at the Mobara plant, was purchased by China's HKC. eLEAP patterns red, green, and blue (RGB) OLED subpixels through a photolithography process without using a fine metal mask (FMM). Its viability for mass production has yet to be verified. The technology is similar in principle to FLiPP, which LG Display unveiled at IMID this August.

The appeal of JDI's eLEAP patents is limited. This is because JDI is reported to have sold licenses (rights of use) for the patents to Applied Materials (AMAT), which makes the deposition equipment required to implement eLEAP, and others. JDI sells the licenses to AMAT and others and collects royalties, which means a third party that buys the patents from JDI cannot use them exclusively. Several panel makers in Korea and abroad are developing eLEAP type technology, but there is little incentive to purchase the JDI patents.

 $MU

items.content:
"Three out of four are defective"... China's CXMT struggles with HBM yields, with immature TSV technology to blame

ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT), China's largest DRAM maker, has begun trial production of fourth generation high bandwidth memory (HBM3), but initial yields are barely improving. Yields are reported to have stalled at 25%, roughly one third of the so called "golden yield" of 80% that the semiconductor industry treats as the threshold for volume production. The gap is stark compared with SK hynix, which has been mass producing the same product since 2022 and has secured yields above 90%. Industry sources point to the gap in maturity of through-silicon via (TSV) technology, the core process for stacking and connecting multiple DRAM layers, as the root cause.

◇ "DRAM has caught up, but HBM stacking is a different problem"

According to a senior official at a semiconductor equipment company familiar with CXMT's situation on the 9th, the yield of CXMT's HBM3 8-High product is stuck at around 30% in the front end process. Of the products that survive that stage, only about 70% are recognized as final good units after passing through the back end process. In simple terms, if 100 HBM3 units are started, close to 80 of them fail the final test.

CXMT is reported to be supplying the small volumes of HBM samples it produces this way to Chinese companies such as Alibaba's T-Head and Cambricon while continuing its yield improvement work. The problem is that the issue does not lie in the fine process technology of the DRAM itself. A semiconductor equipment industry official explained, "There is no major problem with the standard DRAM that CXMT makes on its 'G4' (17nm class) process used for HBM. However, the DRAM dies used for HBM are larger in area than standard products and have more demanding electrical specifications, so even on the same process they are much harder to pass the acceptance criteria."

In other words, CXMT's fundamental capability in making standard DRAM has risen to a considerable level, but a bottleneck is emerging at the stage of converting it into the high performance product that is HBM. At the heart of that bottleneck, according to industry sources, is the TSV process.

◇ The real hurdle is TSV... "Impossible to catch up without years of accumulated know how"

TSV stands for "Through Silicon Via" and refers to the microscopic copper wiring that passes vertically through each layer to carry electrical signals when DRAM is stacked in multiple layers, as in HBM. It is a highly demanding process in which a DRAM wafer is thinned down to several tens of micrometers, a fraction of the thickness of a human hair, after which thousands of tiny holes are drilled through that thin silicon plate and filled completely with copper. A single hole that is misaligned or not properly filled can cause the entire layer to be rejected, making it one of the semiconductor processes with the most stringent precision requirements.

The consensus in the industry is that this is the process where the technology gap between CXMT and the leading companies is widest. According to analysis by semiconductor research firm Nomad Semi, Samsung Electronics' HBM2 (second generation HBM) has more than 5,000 TSVs per die and SK hynix's HBM3 has more than 8,000, while CXMT's is understood to have only around 3,000. A smaller number of TSVs means sacrificing bandwidth (data processing speed) in exchange for lower process difficulty, yet even so CXMT's yields still fall far short of Samsung and SK hynix. TSV is a process that is challenging even for the industry leader: SK hynix itself publicly disclosed in 2024 that the yield of the standalone TSV process was only 40 to 60% at the time.

On top of this, yield losses also occur in the back end (stacking and bonding) stage where the dies are actually stacked and joined. If even one of the eight dies is misaligned, if a microscopic void forms at a bonding interface, or if a layer warps during the thermocompression bonding process (warpage), the entire stack is scrapped. Because the number of possible failure points grows with each additional layer, the difficulty rises exponentially. Given that CXMT is already showing such poor yields at 8-High, some expect it to face even greater difficulties when moving to higher stacks such as 12-High.

A semiconductor industry official explained, "The TSV process is an area that only stabilizes after years of accumulated wafer handling know how. Chinese companies have rapidly closed the gap in the fine process technology of DRAM itself, but back end know how such as TSV and bonding is difficult to catch up on in a short period." He added, "That said, Samsung Electronics also had initial HBM4 (sixth generation HBM) production yields below 60% in February this year and raised them to 80% within six months, so it is too early to declare CXMT's 25% yield a 'failure.'"
— Jukan (@jukan05) Sep 8, 2026
